canonicalExplanation.summary: **Git hooks** are scripts Git runs at certain moments: `pre-commit` before a commit is made, `commit-msg` to check the message, `pre-push` before pushing. They give fast feedback, like formatting staged files in a second. But hooks live in `.git/hooks`, which **isn't cloned**: each developer must install them (for example via a committed launcher like Husky or pre-commit), and anyone can skip them with `--no-verify`. So hooks are a **convenience, not a guarantee**. The **authoritative** checks run in **CI**, on every push. Keep hooks **fast** and put slow suites in pre-push or CI.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A team adds a pre-commit hook that runs the linter and assumes nothing unlinted can reach main. A new teammate never installed the hooks; another used `--no-verify` in a hurry. Main breaks. A versioned hook launcher runs fast formatting checks before commit while authoritative CI reruns all required checks independently. In this lesson you'll design a check placement plan for local, pre-push and CI stages.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Dependencies and reproducible builds**, **Commits and history**, **Formatter and linter** and **Build and task commands**.

sections.heading: The rule: fast locally, complete in CI
sections.body:
```json
// package.json: committed, so everyone gets the same hooks after npm install.
{
  "scripts": { "prepare": "husky" },
  "lint-staged": { "*.{js,ts}": ["prettier --write", "eslint"] }
}
```

```bash
# .husky/pre-commit (committed).
npx lint-staged          # only staged files: about a second.

# .husky/pre-push (committed).
npm test                 # unit tests before sharing.
```

| Stage | Runs | Speed | Can be skipped? |
|---|---|---|---|
| pre-commit. | format + lint staged files. | seconds. | yes (--no-verify). |
| pre-push. | unit tests. | under a minute. | yes. |
| CI. | everything: build, all tests, security scans. | minutes. | no (required checks). |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why not run the full test suite in pre-commit?", "answer": "Slow hooks get skipped with --no-verify, and then they check nothing. Keep commit hooks fast so people leave them on."}
```

includes: Install versioned hooks with a committed launcher and keep them fast.
Place checks across pre-commit, pre-push and CI, treating CI as authoritative.

examples.title: Fast local checks, authoritative CI
examples.situation: A versioned hook launcher runs fast formatting checks before commit while authoritative CI reruns all required checks independently.
walkthrough: **A versioned hook launcher:** Husky config is committed, and npm install sets it up for everyone.
**Runs fast formatting checks before commit:** lint-staged formats and lints staged files in about a second.
**Authoritative CI reruns all required checks independently:** even a --no-verify commit will be caught by CI before merge.
examples.result: Developers get instant feedback, and main is protected regardless of local setups.

examples.title: The five-minute pre-commit
examples.situation: A hook runs the full test suite on every commit. Within a week, everyone commits with --no-verify.
walkthrough: The hook was too slow to keep.
Move the full suite to CI and unit tests to pre-push.
Keep pre-commit to staged-file formatting and lint.
examples.result: Hooks stay on, and feedback stays fast.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: A pre-commit hook guarantees every commit in the remote passed the check and is safe to trust.
misconceptions.correction: Hooks aren't cloned automatically, can be uninstalled, and can be bypassed with --no-verify. Only required server-side checks in CI apply to every push.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening story, how did unlinted code reach main?

analogy.example: Hooks are like **a spell-checker in your own word processor**: quick and helpful, but you can turn it off. CI is **the publisher's editor**, who checks every manuscript before printing, whoever sent it.
usefulFor: remembering your spell-checker vs their editor
fast locally, final at the publisher
limitations: Editors take longer; so does CI.
A writer who disables spell-check still gets caught by the editor.

nearTransfer.prompt: Add a committed pre-commit hook to a sandbox project that formats and lints only staged files. Time it, then commit with --no-verify and explain what that proves about hooks.
scaffold: Husky + lint-staged, or the pre-commit framework.

farTransfer.prompt: Write a check placement plan for a project: list every check (format, lint, types, unit tests, integration tests, secret scan, build), assign each to pre-commit, pre-push or CI with a reason, and mark which are required for merge.
scaffold: CI must include every required check.
expectedEvidence: Every check placed with a reason.

remediation.explanation: For each check ask: **how fast is it, and what happens if someone skips it?** Fast and optional goes local; anything that must hold goes in CI.

recap.summary: To design a check placement plan, install hooks from committed, versioned configuration, keep pre-commit checks fast on staged files, put slower tests in pre-push, and run every required check authoritatively in CI, because local hooks can be missing or bypassed.
